questions.prompt: What is the key difference between `any` and `unknown`?

options.text: They are identical
`any` disables type checking; `unknown` accepts any value but must be narrowed before use
`unknown` disables type checking; `any` must be narrowed
`any` can only hold objects; `unknown` can only hold primitives

questions.explanation: `any` opts a value out of checking. `unknown` is the safe top type: anything is assignable to it, but you must narrow it before using it.

questions.prompt: Does TypeScript have separate types for integers and floating-point numbers?

options.text: Yes — `int` and `float`
No — `number` covers all ordinary numbers; `bigint` exists for very large integers
Yes — `number` for integers and `decimal` for floats
No — every number is a `bigint`

questions.explanation: `number` is a single type for all ordinary numbers. The separate `bigint` type is only for integers beyond the safe range.

questions.prompt: Which are valid ways to type an array of numbers? Select all that apply.

options.text: number[]
Array<number>
[number]
numbers

questions.explanation: number[] and Array<number> are equivalent array types. [number] is a one-element tuple, not a general array.

questions.prompt: When you write `let count = 5`, TypeScript ______ the type as number without an annotation. (one word)
questions.explanation: TypeScript infers a type from the initializer, so an annotation is often unnecessary.

questions.prompt: With strictNullChecks on, does `let name: string = null` compile?

options.text: Yes, null is allowed for any type
No — null isn't assignable to string unless the type includes it (e.g. string | null)
Yes, but only in strict mode
No — string can never hold null even without strict

questions.explanation: Under strictNullChecks, null and undefined stay out of other types; you must widen the type (string | null) to allow null.

questions.prompt: Why is `unknown` the better choice than `any` for the result of JSON.parse?

options.text: It runs faster at runtime
It forces you to check the value's type before using it, preventing silent bugs
It automatically validates the JSON shape
It converts the value to a string

questions.explanation: JSON.parse genuinely returns an unknown shape. Typing it as unknown makes you narrow before use, catching mistakes the compiler would miss with any.
